pharm: Binds the CD20 antigen on the surface of normal and malignant B lymphocytes and mediates B-cell lysis through complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and apoptosis, depleting circulating and tissue B cells
quick: 375 mg/m2 IV per cycle (NHL); 1000 mg IV x2 doses 2 weeks apart (RA/GPA-MPA)
May cause fetal B-cell depletion; avoid - use contraception during and 12 months after
Do not breastfeed during and for 6 months after the last dose
No dose adjustment provided; pharmacokinetics not formally studied
Screen for HBV; reactivation risk - no specific dose adjustment given
Infusion reactions, CBC, HBV serology, signs of PML/infection
summary: Rituximab is an intravenous anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B lymphocytes. It is used for B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (usually 375 mg/m2 per cycle), and for rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis, and pemphigus vulgaris (1000 mg x2 doses). It carries a BOXED WARNING for severe, sometimes fatal mucocutaneous reactions (including toxic epidermal necrolysis), hepatitis B virus (HBV) reactivation that can be fatal, and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Fatal infusion-related reactions can occur, usually with the first infusion - premedicate and infuse slowly. Screen all patients for HBV before treatment.
indications: Relapsed/refractory or previously untreated CD20-positive follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma (single agent or with chemotherapy, including maintenance)
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (CD20-positive) in combination with CHOP or other chemotherapy
Previously untreated and previously treated CD20-positive chronic lymphocytic leukaemia in combination with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide
Moderately-to-severely active rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate after inadequate response to TNF antagonists
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) and microscopic polyangiitis with glucocorticoids

dosage.r: Follicular or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
dosage.d: 375 mg/m2 IV per cycle (with chemotherapy) or weekly x4-8 (single agent); maintenance per protocol
dosage.t: Per chemotherapy cycle or weekly schedule
dosage.n: Start first infusion at 50 mg/h; escalate as tolerated

dosage.d: 375 mg/m2 on day before first chemotherapy cycle, then 500 mg/m2 on day 1 of cycles 2-6 (every 28 days)
dosage.n: Given with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide; tumour lysis prophylaxis

dosage.d: Two 1000 mg IV infusions separated by 2 weeks, repeated every 24 weeks (no sooner than 16 weeks)
dosage.n: Premedicate with methylprednisolone 100 mg IV 30 min before each infusion

dosage.d: 375 mg/m2 IV once weekly for 4 weeks (induction)
1000 mg IV on days 1 and 15, then 500 mg at months 12 and every 6 months thereafter as needed

admin: Intravenous infusion only - never give as IV push or bolus
Premedicate with acetaminophen and an antihistamine before each infusion; add a glucocorticoid in RA/autoimmune indications
Begin first infusion at 50 mg/h; if no reaction escalate in 50 mg/h increments every 30 min to a maximum of 400 mg/h
Interrupt or slow the infusion for infusion reactions; treat and resume at 50% of the previous rate once resolved
Screen for HBV (HBsAg and anti-HBc) before the first dose
Ensure resuscitation facilities and monitoring are available during infusion
moa: Rituximab is a chimeric murine/human monoclonal IgG1 antibody directed against the CD20 antigen expressed on pre-B and mature B lymphocytes. CD20 regulates cell-cycle initiation and differentiation and is not shed or internalised. Binding of rituximab to CD20 triggers complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and induction of apoptosis, resulting in rapid and sustained depletion of circulating and tissue B cells. B-cell recovery generally begins within 6 months of treatment.

absolute: Known severe hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction to rituximab, murine proteins, Chinese hamster ovary cell products or any excipient
relative: Active hepatitis B infection or unresolved HBV serology (high reactivation risk)
Severe heart failure or uncontrolled cardiac disease (infusion-related arrhythmia/angina risk)
monitor: HBV reactivation (during and for several months after therapy)
Signs of serious or opportunistic infection
Tumour lysis syndrome in high tumour-burden disease

preg: Based on its mechanism, rituximab can cause B-cell depletion in the fetus when given during pregnancy. Transient B-cell lymphocytopenia and lymphopenia have been reported in infants exposed in utero. Avoid in pregnancy unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. Females of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for 12 months after the last dose.
lact: There are limited data; rituximab is a large IgG molecule and is likely present in low amounts in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the breastfed infant, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 6 months after the last dose.
renal: No formal pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in renal impairment and no specific dose adjustment is provided. Patients at risk of tumour lysis syndrome (high tumour burden) require renal monitoring and prophylaxis.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is provided for hepatic impairment. All patients must be screened for hepatitis B before treatment because HBV reactivation - sometimes fatal (fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure) - can occur during and for months after therapy; monitor HBV carriers and discontinue if reactivation occurs.

major: Live or live-attenuated vaccines - do not administer during or after rituximab until B-cell recovery (impaired immune response, infection risk)
Other immunosuppressants / biologics - additive immunosuppression and infection risk
moderate: Cisplatin - severe renal toxicity reported when combined in NHL
Antihypertensives - withholding the morning dose may reduce hypotension during infusion
minor: No clinically significant CYP-mediated metabolic interactions (monoclonal antibody)
interactions.diagnostics: Screen HBsAg/anti-HBc before therapy; monitor CBC, immunoglobulins and HBV DNA in at-risk patients

common: Infusion-related reactions (fever, chills, rigors, rash, pruritus, hypotension)
serious: Severe / fatal mucocutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, paraneoplastic pemphigus)
Hepatitis B virus reactivation with fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure and death
rare: Renal toxicity (especially with cisplatin or tumour lysis)
emergency: Anaphylactic / severe infusion reaction with cardiorespiratory compromise
Toxic epidermal necrolysis or severe mucocutaneous reaction

monitoring: Vital signs and infusion reactions during and after each infusion
Hepatitis B serology before therapy; HBV DNA in carriers during and after treatment
Complete blood count at intervals; more frequently with cytopenias
Signs and symptoms of infection and of PML (cognitive, motor or visual changes)
Serum immunoglobulin levels with repeated courses
Renal function and electrolytes in high tumour-burden disease (tumour lysis)
counsel: Infusion reactions are most likely with the first infusion - report fever, chills, breathlessness, rash or itching during the infusion
Report any new or worsening skin rash, blisters or peeling promptly (mucocutaneous reaction)
Tell your team about any history of hepatitis B; you will be screened and may need monitoring for months
Report new weakness, confusion, vision changes or difficulty walking (possible PML)
Report signs of infection (fever, cough, sore throat) and avoid live vaccines
Use effective contraception during and for 12 months after treatment and do not breastfeed during or for 6 months after the last dose
pk: Circulating B cells deplete within days of the first infusion
Serum concentrations are proportional to dose; rise with successive infusions
Mean terminal half-life approximately 18-22 days (varies with dose, indication and tumour burden)
B-cell depletion persists for months; recovery usually begins by 6-9 months and normalises by ~12 months
Refrigerate vials at 2-8 C, protect from light, do not freeze; diluted solution stable refrigerated per label
pearls: BOXED WARNING: severe/fatal mucocutaneous reactions (incl. TEN), HBV reactivation, and PML
Fatal infusion reactions occur mostly with the first infusion - premedicate and start slow at 50 mg/h
Screen every patient for hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc) before the first dose
Suspect PML in any new neurological deficit; stop the drug and image the brain
Tumour lysis prophylaxis and CBC monitoring are essential in high tumour-burden lymphoma/CLL
Avoid live vaccines; vaccinate before therapy when possible because B-cell depletion blunts responses
missed: Rituximab is administered by a healthcare professional on a scheduled basis. If a planned infusion is missed, contact the treating team to reschedule as soon as possible; do not attempt to make up the dose at home.
overdose: There is limited experience with doses above those studied. Manage by immediately interrupting the infusion and providing supportive care; monitor for cytopenias, infusion reactions and cytokine-release symptoms. There is no specific antidote.
